title: Ada-Again and the Time Slip
markdown:
Professor Sel Kestrel kept his office like a timetable: one lamp, one teacup, one faint smell of burnt toast that no one ever quite traced. He was a time-tourism regulator, which meant his days were spent stopping people from inventing disco in ancient Rome or wearing socks with sandals at the French Revolution. The Temporal Authority liked him because he filed on time. Sel liked the Authority because the Authority left him alone. His tweed jacket had a sensible elbow and a more sensible inner pocket for pens that still wrote on the first try.

Sameness, though, made his teacup hand tremble. Doing a thing twice felt like a tiny gremlin leaning into his ear and whispering the same word until the word went sour. He loosened his tweed cuff and told himself the tremor was only the heating. It was not. On quiet afternoons he could almost hear the gremlin practising: again, again, until the office air itself seemed to repeat.

Ada-Again arrived the way a cork leaves a bottle: suddenly, and with more glitter than the room had asked for. She was from Thursday. Not a Thursday. Her Thursday, which she visited the way other people visited a favourite café. She had been in this office before, and before that, and she always looked faintly surprised to find the furniture still here.

“Professor Kestrel,” she said, bells in the voice, mismatched socks already tapping the polish. “Still haven’t found my sparkly purple one.”

“Ada-Again.” Sel pinched the bridge of his nose. “You are Thursday. Today is Thursday.”

“Oh, right.” She giggled. “Silly me. It’s all so… samey, isn’t it?”

The Temporal Authority had begun to sigh down the conduits, a sound like paper being disappointed. If Ada-Again kept folding her own week like pastry, the pasta-pot of paradox would boil over. Worse, from Sel’s chair: he might be assigned to train her on a loop. The same briefing. The same sock. The same Thursday. He would rather face an asteroid. A memo on his console had already used the phrase practical demonstration in a font that meant he was out of excuses.

“Pack your temporal essentials,” he said, and straightened his tie as if the tie could hold the week still. “We’re going to the Titanic.”

Ada-Again clapped. “Is it a bouncy-castle cruise? With tiny sandwiches?”

“It is a significant historical event,” Sel said. “Prepare for the unforgettable.”

He almost did not press the key. Identical decks. Identical waves. A promotion flickering in his mind like a cheap souvenir and then looking, already, like last week’s souvenir. His knees offered to buckle. He breathed the stale office air, tasted defeat, and went anyway. He would not repeat his own flinch.

They arrived in a white flash that left a salt taste on the tongue. The ship loomed, a gleaming cliff of rivets. Tourists in silly hats took pictures with fake icebergs. A brass band somewhere aft was playing a tune that wanted to be cheerful and had not been told about the cold. Ada-Again stared at the water as if water had only just been invented.

“Wow,” she breathed. “Look at all of it. It’s so… wet. And big.”

Sel, professional even with his stomach doing a small mutiny, steered her from the thrill-seekers. The decks repeated themselves: door, rail, door, rail, a geometry that made his teacup hand twitch though he had no teacup. “This is a critical juncture. Observe the safety protocols. Try not to touch anything.” He watched her for the familiar hiccup, the little skip where Thursday folded back on Thursday.

A clumsy tourist bumped her square in the shoulder.

“Oh, pardon me,” Ada-Again said.

A split second later, in the same voice, with the same tilt of the head: “Oh, pardon me.”

Sel’s stomach dropped. He took her arm and pulled her from the thickening crowd. “Focus. This is not a rehearsal for laundry day.”

Near the railing a life raft was going down on ropes that did not quite reach a small huddled group. A child held a threadbare teddy as if the bear were the last solid object in the Atlantic. Someone was crying in a language the tourists’ implants flattened into English and then, unhelpfully, into nothing. Ada-Again drifted toward them on her little loop, pardon me, pardon me, a hypnotic wrong metronome. Sel opened his mouth to shout a warning and felt the old freeze take him: the fear of saying it twice, of being unclear, of repeating his own frantic plea until the words meant nothing. The air tasted of rust and cold iron. The metal of the rail bit his palm. A phantom chill ran his spine, an echo of ice that had not yet arrived and would, in the proper history, arrive anyway.

Ada-Again, still saying pardon me, gave a peculiar almost-graceful twist and leaned into the raft’s path as if the loop itself had found a use for repetition. The ropes caught. The raft slid just enough, its edge kissing the rail where fingers had been grabbing air. Hands found it. The child went aboard with the teddy crushed against a coat, and for one clean second the band aft hit a true note.

“Hooray,” Ada-Again chirped, the loop snapping like a thread. She clapped, delighted and entirely present. “We saved them. I knew this trip would be fun.”

Sel looked at the faces, the wet rail, the ridiculous hats, and then at his own future, which had been a shiny promotion and was now a dinghy drifting off into fog. He took out the temporal log. The device was cold enough to feel like ice waiting below the waterline; salt air pressed close, thick with unanswered warnings. His finger hovered. One entry would deduct her credits and ground her. One entry would also write him out of the quiet rise he had wanted, the escape from the mundane that he had dressed up as ambition. He closed his eyes, took a shaky breath that tasted of rust, and chose the true line.

He typed. Each keystroke sounded small and final, a tiny betrayal of the rise he had wanted and a tiny loyalty to the child on the raft. The bright thing in his mind dissolved the way breath dissolves on a night sea. A hollow ache sat where the hope had been. Under it, oddly, a steadiness: the report would be true. His career path forked, quietly, away from the recognition he had dressed up as escape.

Back at the Temporal Regulation Bureau the silence felt louder than the ship. The burnt-toast smell had been waiting, faithful as a clerk. Sel filed with a new, unshowy certainty. Ada-Again, less sparkly, more subdued, took her penalty notice on official parchment and a credit deduction that would keep her Thursday at home for a good long while. She read it twice, which for her was almost a joke, and did not giggle. They nodded once, a shared, strange acknowledgement, and she went, socks briefly matching in the corridor light before the building swallowed her.

The next day the toast was still there. A temporal alert blinked for a minor glitch in Sector Gamma. In the hallway a bulb stuttered on, off, on, off, a tiny rhythmic stutter that would once have been enough to ruin him. The gremlin leaned in with its favourite word.

Sel looked at the light and smiled, a small crease at the tired corners of his eyes. He stood, walked over, and replaced the bulb. The spent one felt strangely light in his hand, dull and finished. The new one came on in a clean, even hum and laid a steady warmth across the desk, chasing the last of the stale shadow. He sat. The paperwork looked like work again, not a punishment. He drank his tea on the first sip, and did not mind that the cup was the same cup.
characters: Professor Sel Kestrel (a time-tourism regulator), Ada-Again (a repeat visitor from Thursday)
